one_liner: Browser particle demo: the same 16-attractor loop in scalar JavaScript, AssemblyScript and Rust Wasm SIMD, and WebGPU.
what_it_does: A static teaching site ('GPU Playground') that runs one particle simulation four ways: a plain JavaScript loop, an AssemblyScript module and a Rust module compiled to WebAssembly with 128-bit SIMD, and a WebGPU compute shader. The two Wasm modules export the same plain functions (alloc, pointer getters, step) and are driven by one loader, shared/wasm-demo.js, which writes into Wasm memory through Float32Array views; the CPU variants then upload up to 1M positions to a shared WebGL 2 point renderer each frame. It is a reference to read and learn from, not a library: there is no package, API or licence.
how_it_is_fast: The AssemblyScript step (2-wasm/assembly/index.ts) keeps x, y, vx and vy as separate f32 arrays (structure of arrays) and updates 4 particles per instruction with f32x4 load, sub, mul, div and store, against JavaScript's scalar loop that does the same maths one particle at a time in f64. Built with asc 0.28.20 (binaryen 131 nightly per package-lock.json) using --optimize --noAssert --runtime stub, so there are no bounds checks or GC runtime in the hot loop. Most of the gap is therefore SIMD width plus f32 arithmetic, not AssemblyScript as a language.
when_to_use: Learning or teaching where browser compute time goes: the same kernel side by side in JS, Wasm SIMD (AssemblyScript and Rust) and WebGPU, with a per-step CPU-time bar in each demo.
Deciding whether a compute-heavy per-element f32 loop (about 16 divisions per element per frame) at 1M to 4M elements is worth porting from JavaScript to Wasm SIMD.
As a template for loading an AssemblyScript or Rust (no wasm-bindgen) module through plain exports and sharing arrays with JavaScript via typed-array views into Wasm memory.
when_not_to_use: As code to vendor: the repository has no licence file, so reuse is not granted.

If you need trustworthy numbers: the README reports only frame rates on an unnamed Apple Silicon Mac in an unnamed browser, capped at 60 fps, with no Light-mode figures and none of the per-step sim timings the HUD displays.

If you are choosing AssemblyScript for speed: the project's own table has its Rust Wasm build ahead of AssemblyScript at every size (60/41/11 fps against 40/37/6) and the README puts Rust's step about 15% faster in Light mode.
For millions of particles at interactive rates: only the WebGPU variant holds 60 fps at 4M (about 48 at 16M); every CPU variant also pays a CPU-to-GPU copy each frame.
Browsers without Wasm SIMD (simd128) or WebGL 2.

integration.dependencies: none at run time (any static HTTP server; npm start uses python3 -m http.server); rebuilding needs assemblyscript 0.28.20 (npm) and a Rust toolchain with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript 0.28.20; Rust edition 2024 crate (Rust 1.85+); browser with Wasm SIMD and WebGL 2, WebGPU for demo 3
integration.platforms: any desktop browser with Wasm simd128; measured only on an Apple Silicon Mac
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded; both modules keep particle state in module globals (Rust uses static mut and documents the one-thread assumption)

gotchas: The JavaScript baseline computes in f64 and rounds on each Float32Array store, while both Wasm builds compute in f32 SIMD, so trajectories differ slightly from the JS demo; the README's 'identical results' refers to AssemblyScript against Rust only.

The AssemblyScript row is internally inconsistent (40 fps at 1M against 37 fps at 4M for four times the work, while JS and Rust scale with work), so the 1M reading, and the 1.2x ratio derived from it, is unreliable; the 4M pair (8 against 37 fps, about 4.6x) is the usable comparison and is a lower bound on the step-time ratio because both frames include the same 1M-point upload and draw.

Harness flaw in shared/ui.js: changing the particle count clears the sample window but not lastFrame, so the first frame after a switch carries the whole allocation and re-seeding pause; the overview page shows whichever reading was saved last (saved at most once a second once 10 samples exist), so a reading taken soon after a switch understates fps.

The AssemblyScript module uses --runtime stub with hand-managed pointers after __heap_base: memory grows but is never freed, and JavaScript must rebuild its typed-array views after every alloc because memory.grow replaces the buffer (wasm-demo.js does this).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over wasm-perf (Emscripten C SIMD matrix multiply against Node) or AutoZig (Zig SIMD image filter) when you want an in-browser, AssemblyScript-specific comparison that also shows the Rust Wasm and WebGPU alternatives on the same kernel; for measured, scriptable numbers those siblings' command-line benchmarks are easier to reproduce.
verified_claims_summary: Heavy mode (16 attractors), unnamed Apple Silicon Mac and browser, whole-frame rates averaged over the last 30 requestAnimationFrame frames: scalar JavaScript 33 fps at 1M and 8 fps at 4M particles against AssemblyScript f32x4 Wasm (asc 0.28.20) 40 and 37 fps (about 1.2x and 4.6x, derived from page data), with Rust Wasm 60/41/11 and WebGPU 60/60/~48 fps at 1M/4M/16M; every CPU variant includes the same WebGL upload and draw of at most 1M points.
status_note: Single-commit study repository (2026-10-09, 0 stars) with no licence file, so it is a reference to read rather than code to copy; both compiled .wasm files are checked in and contain the expected f32x4 SIMD instructions.
